newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Jockey Club pulls major account from Jardines.
newsitem.headline: HK's Jockey Club pulls major account from Jardines.

text.p: The Hong Kong Jockey Club said on Thursday it has withdrawn HK$1 billion (US$129 million) from scandal-tainted Jardine Fleming Investment Management.
"We have served notice to terminate the retirement scheme with Jardines," said Paulus Lee, director of the Jockey Club's finance and central services.
Lee warned that two other major Jockey Club accounts, the contingency fund and the charities trust fund, will stay under JFIM's management for now, but this will be subject to review next March.
"We have a semi-annual review process for all our fund managers, and like the rest of them they will continue to be under review," he said. "Obviously, (the scandal) has some input."

The withdrawal of retirement funds by an old and leading Hong Kong body underlines the continuing upheaval at Jardine Fleming Holdings Ltd, part of one of the territory's most established financial institutions.

A trading scandal involving the chief investment officer at the company's fund management subsidiary provoked heavy regulatory penalties last month and a rash of resignations, culminating in the departure of company chairman Alan Smith last week.

Jardine Fleming officials in London conceded last month that US$3 billion in assets could be compromised by the scandal, which prompted the immediate removal by investors of between US$50 million and US$100 million in funds, they said.
Jardine Fleming responded with a radical corporate restructuring that included a new supervisory board as well as hefty reinforcements to its compliance division.

Jardine Fleming had no comment on reports it had already lost two portfolios valued at 21.5 million sterling (US$33.5 million) each with the United Kingdom's Civil Aviation Authority, or that the US$32.4 billion IBM United Kingdom Pension Trust was reconsidering JFIM's management mandate.
"We have lost some accounts, as we always expected we would," a company spokesman said.
But he denied accounts were leaving thick and fast. Up to US$1 billion in new money from Japan would replace any accounts that were lost, he said.
Competitors declined to comment on the significance of the decision by the Jockey Club, which enjoys a special status in Hong Kong.
But rival fund management companies said they were starting to reap some slight gains at JFIM's expense, as former clients looked for new money managers.
"There hasn't been much switchover," said a senior official at Schroders Investment Management. "But I'd rather not comment on the misfortunes of others."

Regulators hit Jardine Fleming with a fine of 700,000 sterling (US$1.09 million) and withdrew the authorisation of its London-based fund company last month following revelations of the late allocation of trades by Colin Armstrong. Many of the trades involved his personal account.
Jardine Fleming paid US$19.3 million in compensation to disadvantaged clients. Armstrong contributed to the payment.
Jardine Fleming Holdings Ltd is jointly owned by Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd and the Robert Fleming group.
